lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Tiresias, whether you’re actually blind or not is hard to say now. We’ve all got the exact same empty sockets down here. You can’t tell Phineus the blind man from Lynceus the eagle-eyed. But the poets tell me you were a prophet, and the only person to have lived as both a man and a woman. So, by the gods, tell me: which life was better? The male or the female?

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: The female, Menippus, by far. It’s so much less trouble. Women rule over men, and they don’t have to go to war, or stand on the battlements, or argue in the assembly, or be cross-examined in the courts.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: You obviously haven’t heard Euripides’ *Medea*, Tiresias. She goes on and on about how wretched women are, and the unbearable agony of childbirth. But tell me—speaking of Medea—did you ever give birth when you were a woman? Or did you remain barren and childless in that life?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: It's a simple question, Tiresias. Just answer it, if you don't mind.

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: I was not barren, but I did not give birth.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: That’s all I needed. I just wanted to know if you had a womb.

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: Of course I had a womb.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: And did it fade away over time? Did the female parts seal up, the breasts drop off, the male parts sprout, and a beard push its way out? Or did you turn from a woman into a man all at once?

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: I fail to see the point of this interrogation. [pause] You seem to doubt this happened at all.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: What, I’m not supposed to doubt things like this, Tiresias? I should just swallow it like an idiot, without asking whether it’s actually possible?

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: I suppose you don't believe the other stories either, then? When you hear about women turning into birds or trees or beasts—Aedon, Daphne, Lycaon's daughter?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: If I ever run into them, I'll see what they have to say for themselves. But back to you, my good man. When you were a woman, were you a prophet then too? Or did you learn to be a man and a prophet at the same time?

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: You see? You know absolutely nothing about my story! I settled a dispute between the gods. Hera struck me blind in anger, and Zeus compensated me with the gift of prophecy.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Still clinging to the fables, Tiresias? Ah well, you're just acting like a prophet. It's practically your job description never to tell the truth.
